messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Mateo Reyes was twenty-one years old when his National Guard unit was deployed to a forward operating base in eastern Afghanistan. He had enlisted partly to help pay for college and partly because his father, a Salvadoran immigrant who had built a small accounting firm from nothing, had spoken often about duty and sacrifice. Mateo had been proud of the uniform. By the time he came home eighteen months later, that pride had become something he could no longer locate inside himself.

The event that reorganized Mateo's inner life occurred during a patrol in a narrow valley corridor on a morning that had begun unremarkably. His unit came under sustained fire from elevated positions on both sides of the ridgeline. In the chaos that followed, Mateo made a series of decisions — he describes them haltingly, in fragments, never in sequence — that resulted in the death of a fellow soldier and, separately, in actions he took that he has never been able to fully narrate aloud. What he can say is that the air smelled like burning diesel and that the sky was enormous and open above the valley, offering no cover, no shelter, nothing but exposure in every direction. He remembers the color of the light. He remembers a sound. The rest arrives in pieces, out of order, and he has never been able to assemble them into a story that makes sense to him.

After his discharge, Mateo enrolled in a finance program and graduated, finding work as a financial analyst at a mid-sized firm in Houston. On paper, the transition looked successful. Internally, it was not. The memories did not organize themselves with time. Vivid, detailed fragments surfaced without warning — a texture, a color, the particular quality of open sky — and then vanished before he could examine them, leaving him disoriented at his desk, staring at spreadsheets he could not read. His firm's office occupies a high floor with floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking a wide plaza, and on days when the light falls a certain way across that open expanse below, Mateo has had to excuse himself to the men's room and wait for the intrusion to pass. He had come to dread clear days more than overcast ones. He had rearranged his desk so that his back faced the windows.

He stopped attending the informal Friday gatherings his colleagues organized at a nearby bar, then stopped joining team lunches, then began eating at his desk with headphones in. His manager noticed and asked twice if everything was alright. Mateo said yes both times. He was certain that if he began talking about what had happened, something irreversible would occur — not a breakdown exactly, but a confirmation of what he already suspected about himself: that the person who had come back from that valley was not someone who belonged in ordinary life. He had come to believe, with a quiet and terrible certainty, that he simply did not have a future in the way other people did — not a retirement, not a family, not the accounting firm his father had once joked Mateo might inherit. Those possibilities felt like they belonged to someone else's timeline.

What frightened him most was not the memories themselves but what he understood them to mean about who he was. He had acted in ways that violated something central to how he had always understood himself — his sense of fairness, of protection, of what a person owed to the people beside them. He did not discuss this with anyone. A photograph of his unit, which his mother had framed and placed in his childhood bedroom, now lived face-down in a drawer. He had not visited his parents in four months, unwilling to sit in that room.

What finally brought Mateo to the clinic was a performance review in which his manager noted, gently but formally, that his engagement with the team had significantly declined. He sat in the parking garage afterward and understood that the life he was trying to hold together was contracting. He arrived at the intake appointment quiet and precise, answering questions carefully. What he said he was hoping for, after a long pause, was simply to be able to sit near a window again without feeling like the sky was something to be afraid of.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Avoid Grief Reminders: The vignette shows Mateo avoiding a photograph of his unit (placed face-down in a drawer) and avoiding his parents' home, but these are framed as avoidance of guilt/shame reminders rather than reminders of someone he has lost. The core content — avoiding things that remind him of a person he has lost (grief over a specific loss) — is not clearly reflected.: The patient's 'Avoid Grief Reminders' symptom specifically references avoiding anything that reminds them of someone they have lost, indicating grief-focused avoidance tied to bereavement. While the vignette mentions the death of a fellow soldier and Mateo avoiding the unit photograph and his parents' home, these are framed primarily around shame and self-concept violation rather than grief over a lost person. The vignette does not clearly portray Mateo steering away from reminders of the deceased soldier as a grief response, which is the core of this symptom item.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

Mateo Reyes was twenty-one years old when his National Guard unit was deployed to a forward operating base in eastern Afghanistan. He had enlisted partly to help pay for college and partly because his father, a Salvadoran immigrant who had built a small accounting firm from nothing, had spoken often about duty and sacrifice. Mateo had been proud of the uniform. By the time he came home eighteen months later, that pride had become something he could no longer locate inside himself.

The event that reorganized Mateo's inner life occurred during a patrol in a narrow valley corridor on a morning that had begun unremarkably. His unit came under sustained fire from elevated positions on both sides of the ridgeline. In the chaos that followed, Mateo made a series of decisions — he describes them haltingly, in fragments, never in sequence — that resulted in the death of a fellow soldier named Darnell, a twenty-three-year-old from Beaumont who had been in Mateo's fire team since basic training and who had, the night before the patrol, lent Mateo a paperback novel and told him a long, meandering story about his younger sister's quinceañera plans. Separately, in the same engagement, Mateo took actions he has never been able to fully narrate aloud. What he can say is that the air smelled like burning diesel and that the sky was enormous and open above the valley, offering no cover, no shelter, nothing but exposure in every direction. He remembers the color of the light. He remembers a sound. The rest arrives in pieces, out of order, and he has never been able to assemble them into a story that makes sense to him.

After his discharge, Mateo enrolled in a finance program and graduated, finding work as a financial analyst at a mid-sized firm in Houston. On paper, the transition looked successful. Internally, it was not. The memories did not organize themselves with time. Vivid, detailed fragments surfaced without warning — a texture, a color, the particular quality of open sky — and then vanished before he could examine them, leaving him disoriented at his desk, staring at spreadsheets he could not read. His firm's office occupies a high floor with floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking a wide plaza, and on days when the light falls a certain way across that open expanse below, Mateo has had to excuse himself to the men's room and wait for the intrusion to pass. He had come to dread clear days more than overcast ones. He had rearranged his desk so that his back faced the windows. In the months after his return, grief over Darnell had settled into his daily life in ways that were quiet and cumulative. He had deleted the thread of text messages between them rather than read them again. He had stopped listening to the playlist Darnell had shared with the whole team during their downtime at the FOB, and when a song from it surfaced on a streaming service's auto-generated queue one evening, he closed the app and sat in silence for the remainder of the night. A photograph of his unit, which his mother had framed and placed in his childhood bedroom, now lived face-down in a drawer — not only because of what it said about who Mateo had been in that valley, but because Darnell was in it, standing at the left edge of the frame with his arm around Mateo's shoulder, and looking at it felt like pressing on something that had no bottom. He had not visited his parents in four months, unwilling to sit in that room.

He stopped attending the informal Friday gatherings his colleagues organized at a nearby bar, then stopped joining team lunches, then began eating at his desk with headphones in. His manager noticed and asked twice if everything was alright. Mateo said yes both times. He was certain that if he began talking about what had happened, something irreversible would occur — not a breakdown exactly, but a confirmation of what he already suspected about himself: that the person who had come back from that valley was not someone who belonged in ordinary life. He had come to believe, with a quiet and terrible certainty, that he simply did not have a future in the way other people did — not a retirement, not a family, not the accounting firm his father had once joked Mateo might inherit. Those possibilities felt like they belonged to someone else's timeline. What frightened him most was not the memories themselves but what he understood them to mean about who he was. He had acted in ways that violated something central to how he had always understood himself — his sense of fairness, of protection, of what a person owed to the people beside them. He did not discuss this with anyone.

What finally brought Mateo to the clinic was a performance review in which his manager noted, gently but formally, that his engagement with the team had significantly declined. He sat in the parking garage afterward and understood that the life he was trying to hold together was contracting. He arrived at the intake appointment quiet and precise, answering questions carefully. What he said he was hoping for, after a long pause, was simply to be able to sit near a window again without feeling like the sky was something to be afraid of.
